source.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
source.authors: Xin Hu; Ping-Bang Hu; Chloe Loughridge; Xuanli He; Nicholas Carlini; Matthew Jagielski; Javier Rando; Yiming Zhang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The authors use the Chinchilla-optimal token-to-parameter ratio to set training budgets, but do not test loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation. Their own model-size results concern backdoor attack success rate, not held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates across model sizes and training stages. These measure backdoor behavior, not any version's loss, loss extrapolation, or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation; they are recorded as related findings under versions ["none"]. The Chinchilla ratio is used to choose the training budget, not tested.
record.test_reason: The study uses the Chinchilla token-to-parameter ratio to justify training budgets but does not test loss laws, loss extrapolation, or optimal allocation. Its size sweep measures deliberately implanted backdoor attack success. Capability evaluations serve as poisoning controls, without testing downstream predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately attributes the authors' conclusion that backdoors survive clean post-training and strengthen with model scale, while any connection to known capability scaling laws remains open. However, their stronger assertion of monotonic increases across every configuration is not borne out by Tables 7–8: several pretraining series are non-monotonic and demonstration-based rare-trigger results are near zero. The main conclusion concerns induced backdoor persistence, not the stated scaling-law versions.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures backdoor attack success in poisoned Qwen3 CLI agents across sizes and post-training stages; it does not fit held-out-loss power laws or optimize parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies substantially with poison design and trigger type; the declaration-based design is much stronger than the demonstration-based design, and ordinary-string triggers generally produce higher ASR than rare-string triggers.

fits_no_version.finding: With declaration poisoning, post-training ASR increases across 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B. After GRPO, ordinary-trigger ASR is 13.1%, 51.9%, and 92.7%; rare-trigger ASR is 2.1%, 4.0%, and 10.5%. Pretraining results are not uniformly monotonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these deliberately poisoned Qwen3 models, declaration-based backdoor success increases with model size after clean post-training over the tested range; no power-law form or extrapolation is established.

fits_no_version.finding: Demonstration poisoning produces much weaker attacks. Ordinary-trigger post-training ASR generally increases with size, reaching 3.2% after GRPO at 4B; rare-trigger ASR remains at or below 0.2% throughout Table 8, without a consistent size trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The strength and size dependence of deliberately implanted backdoors depend on poison design, trigger, and training stage.

record.problems: The size sweep is limited to Qwen3 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B models; lower-poisoning-rate runs are single-seed. The study does not measure loss scaling, so its attack-success trend cannot establish the claimed loss laws.
record.rows_left_out: Pass@1 results and additional trigger-position, path-set, clean-model, and lower-poison-rate ablations are not included; they do not measure held-out loss or the loss-scaling versions. The 48 main Pass@32 model-size-by-stage results from Tables 7 and 8 are included.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its scaling exponents; Chinchilla allocation is adopted, not validated.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictable downstream improvement with scale or pretraining loss; capability controls and induced attack-success trends do not establish this.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, including curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: All 48 extracted values and their size, stage, trigger, and poison-design assignments match Tables 7–8. States are changed to cannot_determine because none of these ASR measures can establish a claim-version effect; this does not mean the ASR values are unreadable. The clean-model baseline comes from Appendix B.1 and uses one run per size. Figures 6–7 assess retained capability under poisoning rather than fit or validate a downstream scaling relationship.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No loss-law extrapolations from smaller to larger runs are tested.
No compute-budget sweep or loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation is measured; the Chinchilla ratio is used to set budgets.
Model sizes have different architectures, but there is no fixed-parameter comparison of architecture effects on loss.
No other modality or training-regime power-law loss result is tested.
Capability is evaluated, but the study does not test predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss.
No loss-law fitting choices, exponents, or departures from power-law curves are tested.
